title: The tangle
hookLine: a tangle within, a tangle without; who untangles it? one grounded in virtue (SN 1.23)

lines: PULL ONE, THREE COME WITH IT.
NOW MAKE THE DRAWER A LIFE.
cards: Open a drawer of old charging cables. Pull one, and three others come with it. Pull harder, and the knot tightens.
What works is the opposite: stop pulling, find one loose end, and slowly work it free. Now make the drawer a life.

A money worry wrapped around a fight with your sister, wrapped around a habit you can't drop, wrapped around the news. That's the picture a deva brings to the Buddha in a discourse of just two verses.

teach.h: A TANGLE WITHIN, A TANGLE WITHOUT
teach.b: SN 1.23 is two verses. The deva asks: a tangle within, a tangle without, this whole generation is tangled in a tangle. I ask you this, Gotama: who can untangle this tangle?
Within: our cravings and fears. Without: the people and things we're caught up with.
The Pali word is jata, also used for matted hair, the kind wandering ascetics let grow into ropes. A tangle you don't make all at once, and can't comb out all at once either.

The Buddha answers with three things: a person established in virtue, developing the mind, meaning steady attention, and wisdom. Someone ardent and discerning, with those three, can untangle this tangle.
The order matters. You don't start with the hardest knot. You start by not adding new ones, which is what virtue does: no new lies to keep straight, no new harm to undo.
Then attention steadies the hands. Then wisdom sees where the strands actually run.

teach.h: THE OPENING OF THE PATH OF PURIFICATION
teach.b: Much later, the commentator Buddhaghosa opened his huge handbook, the Path of Purification, with this exact verse, and built the whole book on the three: virtue, concentration, wisdom.
One deva's question became the outline of a book Theravada students still study closely.
And the answer never promises the tangle disappears in a day. It names who can work it loose.

how: Theravada monastics and some lay students study Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, which opens with the tangle verse of SN 1.23 and is arranged as virtue, concentration and wisdom.

o: a rope that binds beings to rebirth
knots of craving, inside us and out
a riddle the Buddha set to test monks

s: Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification opens with the tangle verse
he built the whole handbook on virtue, concentration and wisdom.
the tangle in SN 1.23 is only inside the mind
the deva asks about a tangle within and a tangle without.
the Buddha promises the tangle disappears all at once
he names the kind of person who can work it loose: grounded in virtue, steady and wise.

games.q: you're facing a tangled life: old habits, hard relationships, worries. by SN 1.23, where do you start?
o: with the biggest knot, all at once.
with virtue: stop tying new knots.
by cutting everything loose and walking away.
games.why: the answer begins with someone established in virtue, then a developed mind, then wisdom. the order starts with not adding new knots.

practice: Let one small knot come to mind, not the biggest: an unanswered message, a misunderstanding, a pile you keep stepping around.

Don't pull on it; just look, the way you'd look at a knotted cable before touching it, and ask where one loose end might be. Let the smallest first move show itself, a one-line reply, one honest sentence, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: The tangle. Jata: the knot within and without, from SN 1.23, untangled by virtue, a steady mind, and wisdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali jata: a tangle, or matted, knotted hair. SN 1.23 is the Jata Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: tangle within, tangle without. Virtue first, then a steady mind, then wisdom. Day six hundred thirty-nine, done.
